items.title: Explainer: What to know about Russia-U.S.-Ukraine trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi
text: ABU DHABI, Nov. 11 (Xinhua) -- Trilateral talks involving Russia, the United States and Ukraine ended on Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), with Russia and Ukraine reaching an agreement on a "large-scale" prisoner exchange.
While the agreement marked a tangible outcome of the two-day discussions, no agreement was announced on a ceasefire, territorial disputes or long-term security guarantees.
What did the two-day talks achieve, and what are the prospects for further negotiations?
Vladimir Medinsky, head of the Russian delegation, said the delegations had discussed humanitarian issues, with the future of European security being a central focus of the U.S.-mediated talks.
He added that the parties had reached understandings on some issues, without providing further details.
Medinsky called for a fair security framework that takes into account the interests of all countries, arguing that the conflict in Ukraine had exposed shortcomings in Europe's security system.
Jared Kushner, a member of the U.S. negotiating team, told reporters that the discussions were thorough and covered all major issues, which he described as a good first step forward.
He noted that the prisoner exchange deal was one of the positive outcomes of the negotiations, with the exact number of prisoners to be finalized on Thursday.

On the Ukrainian side, negotiator David Arakhamia, chairman of the Servant of the People parliamentary faction, a Ukrainian political party, said the talks had generated "good momentum" toward finding a solution to the conflict before the end of the year.
Although progress was reported on the prisoner exchange, no agreement was announced on a ceasefire, territorial disputes or long-term security guarantees.
Vadim Kozyulin, chief researcher at the Institute of Contemporary International Studies of the Russian Diplomatic Academy, said the parties appeared ready to negotiate but not to make concessions.

He noted that the parties had fundamentally different understandings of security guarantees. While Kyiv seeks firm commitments to protect Ukraine, Moscow insists that Ukraine's security should not come at the expense of Russia's.
Progress would depend on whether they were willing to discuss mutual obligations rather than simply reiterate their own demands, Kozyulin said.
Ahmed Al-Janabi, a UAE political analyst, described the talks as a significant step toward a political settlement, saying they had helped revive diplomatic engagement between Moscow and Kyiv.
He noted that the conflict was rooted partly in competing views over Ukraine's place in Europe's security architecture, its relationship with NATO and territorial disputes with Russia.

Any agreement failing to address the underlying causes of the conflict and provide acceptable security arrangements would remain fragile, said Al-Janabi, adding that a lasting settlement would require mutual concessions and clear guarantees to prevent renewed hostilities.
Kushner said he and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff planned to travel to Moscow for further discussions.

items.title: Chinese FM holds positive, constructive phone talks with Rubio on China-U.S. ties
text: BEIJING, Nov. 11 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Wednesday held positive and constructive phone talks with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The two sides had an in-depth exchange of views on China-U.S. relations and the interaction between the two heads of state.

During the talks, Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that President Xi Jinping's visit to the United States in September was smooth and successful.

The two heads of state agreed to enrich the connotation of a new vision of China-U.S. relations, providing clearer strategic guidance for exploring a right approach for the two countries to get along with each other, Wang said.
The stable momentum of China-U.S. relations has not come easily and is the two major countries' rational choice based on their respective and common interests, Wang said.

China, having maintained a stable and consistent policy towards the United States, is willing to strengthen communication and cooperation with the U.S. side, properly handle differences and sensitive issues, support each other in hosting the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting and the G20 Summit, and work to bring a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability into effect and deliver results, Wang said.  ■

Former deserted Chinese mining sites star again via "lights, camera, action"
text: YINCHUAN, Nov. 12 (Xinhua) -- Weathered red brick factory buildings, rusted doors and windows, and faded slogans have not prevented a once-deserted mine in northwest China from becoming a must-see destination for tourists, particularly movie fans.

With a complete set of mining and other relevant facilities that operated for 30 years, and located next to diverse landforms including canyons and desert, the Shitanjing mining site in the city of Shizuishan, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, has attracted nearly 60 film crews, particularly for suspense, military and sci-fi movie productions.

Another hit movie added to the site's charm in the summer of 2026. "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East," which filmed a quarter of its exterior scenes in Shitanjing, has been selected by the Chinese mainland as its official entry for the Best International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards.

"The peak number of tourists in Shitanjing reached 10,000 in a single day after the movie was released," said Wang Peng, an official of the Shitanjing subdistrict, adding that the site has received over 370,000 tourists in the first 10 months of this year, an increase of about 160 percent year on year.

"Many visitors thought the scenes were filmed abroad, but they were actually in the mining area where we grew up," said Ge Yihong, a 64-year-old local resident. She has become a "living map" of Shitanjing, helping film crews scout filming locations and providing free guiding services to tourists.

Shitanjing was one of the ten major coal industry bases planned by China during the first Five-Year Plan period (1953-1957). At its peak, 130,000 people from all over the country lived there, with factories, shopping malls, schools, cinemas and other facilities readily available.

Starting in 2002, the gradual closure of mining areas, driven by industrial structure adjustment and strategic resource protection, caused the population to drop sharply, and the site fell into decline for a period.

A turning point came in 2017, when Ningxia rolled out an ecological protection and restoration program for the Helan Mountains, home to the site. Tourists and veteran miners began to visit the site, while film crews started scouting it for shooting locations.

"Complete mining and supporting facilities from the 1960s to the 1990s are well preserved here, including factories, dormitories and stations, offering authentic scenes and a strong atmosphere for film crews," said Zhu Yuhong, director of the bureau of culture, sports, tourism, radio, film and television of the Dawukou District, which administers the site.

Shizuishan launched efforts in 2021 to develop Shitanjing into a tourism destination centered on industrial tourism and filmmaking. An actors' guild was also established at the site, providing more than 13,000 extras for film crews.
Ge opened a restaurant at the site last year. "With the growing number of tourists, daily turnover can reach as much as 2,000 yuan (around 298 U.S. dollars)," she said.

items.title: Xi calls for carrying forward Sun Yat-sen's legacy in national rejuvenation drive
text: BEIJING, Nov. 12 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday called for carrying forward the legacy of Sun Yat-sen, one of the nation's revered revolutionary forefathers, to make joint efforts for national rejuvenation and turn into reality the great dream of all Chinese people since the advent of modern times.

Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks at a gathering held in Beijing to commemorate the 160th anniversary of Sun's birth.
Born in 1866, Sun led the Revolution of 1911 more than a century ago to abolish the absolute monarchy that had ruled China for thousands of years. Sun died in 1925.
Addressing the event in the Great Hall of the People, Xi hailed Sun as a great national hero, a great patriot and a great pioneer of China's democratic revolution.
Xi noted that Chinese communists are the most steadfast supporters, loyal collaborators, and faithful successors to the revolutionary cause initiated by Sun.
For more than 100 years, the CPC has led the Chinese people in writing the most magnificent chapter in the history of the Chinese nation, Xi said.
"The best way for us to remember Dr. Sun is to emulate, inherit and carry forward his invaluable spirit, steadily advancing our endeavors to build a great country and rejuvenate our nation," Xi said.
Highlighting Sun's lifelong devotion to the country, Xi called on all Chinese people to learn from Sun and promote patriotism to strive for a strong and prosperous China.
He also lauded Sun's dedication to the people, underscoring the imperative of always putting the people first and serving them wholeheartedly.
On the new journey, it is essential to make solid headway in promoting well-rounded personal development and common prosperity for all, Xi stressed.

Noting that Sun devoted his life to the pursuit of truth, Xi stressed the need to learn from Sun's example, advance theoretical exploration and innovation with courage, and continue to write new chapters in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of the times.
Xi called on the Chinese people to carry forward Sun's unyielding determination, rise to challenges ahead and break new ground in the country's development.

"We must carry forward the fighting spirit, build up our ability, be ready to withstand high winds, choppy waters, and even dangerous storms, and overcome all the risks and challenges we face on the way forward," Xi said.
Calling on people to learn from Sun's commitment to unity, Xi also emphasized adhering to the united front and strengthening the great unity among all the sons and daughters of the Chinese nation.
Highlighting Sun's global vision, Xi called for vigorously promoting the common values of humanity and actively advancing the building of a community with a shared future for humanity.
"Dr. Sun always upheld national unity and ethnic solidarity, and resolutely opposed any word or act attempting to split the country and divide the nation," Xi said.

items.title: Chinese VP meets Turkish president
text: Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, as President Xi Jinping's special representative, meets with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on the sidelines of the Antalya Leaders' Summit of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, Nov. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Liu Weibing)

ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov. 11 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, as President Xi Jinping's special representative, met with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Wednesday on the sidelines of the Antalya Leaders' Summit of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31).
Conveying Xi's cordial greetings and best wishes to Erdogan, Han said that China and Türkiye enjoy a long history of friendly exchanges.

Under the strategic guidance of Xi and Erdogan, China-Türkiye relations have maintained sound and steady development, Han said, noting that China stands ready to work with Türkiye to advance high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, deepen practical cooperation across various fields, and promote the continuous development of the China-Türkiye strategic cooperative relationship.

Noting that the two heads of state have reached an important political consensus on accommodating each other's core interests and major concerns, Han said the two sides should support each other in pursuing the paths chosen by their own people and safeguarding their respective national sovereignty, security and development interests.

The two countries should elevate the level of practical cooperation, he said, stressing that China is ready to encourage more Chinese enterprises to invest and start businesses in Türkiye in line with market-oriented and commercial principles.

The two sides enjoy broad prospects for cooperation in renewable energy, artificial intelligence, biotechnology and other fields, and can jointly create more highlights in bilateral cooperation, Han added.
China appreciates Türkiye's efforts to advance global climate governance, and stands ready to work with Türkiye to ensure the success of COP31, the Chinese vice president said.
Erdogan, for his part, asked Han to convey his sincere greetings and best wishes to Xi.
He said that Türkiye attaches great importance to developing relations with China and firmly adheres to the one-China principle.
The Turkish president recalled that he met with Xi and reached a new consensus to promote the development of Türkiye-China relations at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Tianjin Summit last year.

Türkiye is willing to firmly promote the implementation of the consensus, maintain close high-level exchanges with China, advance high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, enhance trade and investment, expand cooperation in new energy, minerals, artificial intelligence, transportation, tourism and other fields, promote people-to-people exchanges, and elevate Türkiye-China relations to a new level, said Erdogan.

He noted that Türkiye appreciates China's important contributions to promoting world peace and development, and hopes to enhance communication and collaboration with China to jointly promote peace and stability in the Middle East and work together to address global challenges such as climate change.

items.title: China voices support for UN Early Warnings for All initiative
text: ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov. 11 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice President Han Zheng on Wednesday said that China firmly supports the UN Early Warnings for All initiative, calling on all countries to work together and take joint action.
Han made the remarks at a high-level event for the UN Early Warnings for All initiative in Antalya, Türkiye, hosted by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.

He said that as climate change continues to intensify and a super El Nino heightens the risk of extreme weather worldwide, building inclusive and efficient early warning systems is an effective way to address the climate crisis.
The Chinese vice president put forward three proposals.

First, strengthen the early warning network. In July, Chinese President Xi Jinping announced at the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference that China would promote and deploy its "MAZU" intelligent meteorological early warning system in 30 countries over the next five years, according to Han.

China stands ready to accelerate the deployment of the "MAZU" solution in more developing countries, integrate all stages of the early warning process, from risk identification, monitoring and forecasting, and warning dissemination to emergency response, and help countries of the Global South establish autonomous, controllable and sustainable early warning systems, he said.

Second, enhance science and technology empowerment. China has actively provided early warning equipment to developing countries and supplied more than 200 types of cloud-based early warning service products to over 50 countries, he said.

China is willing to leverage technologies such as meteorological satellites and intelligent forecasting to better support meteorological monitoring, risk assessment and warning dissemination, enhance early warning capabilities, and translate advanced technologies into tangible, practical results in disaster prevention and mitigation, he noted.

Third, bolster capacity building. China is prepared to further enhance early warning training for developing countries, promote experience sharing, technical exchanges and personnel visits, and help developing countries cultivate local teams of professionals, Han said.

He stressed that China will continue to support and participate in relevant activities under the UN Early Warnings for All initiative, and work with other countries to address climate challenges, strengthen climate resilience and safeguard people's safety.

items.title: Chinese VP attends COP31 Antalya Leaders' Summit
text: ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov. 11 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, as President Xi Jinping's special representative, attended the Antalya Leaders' Summit of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) on Wednesday and delivered a national statement.
Han said that Xi has pointed out that responding to climate change is the common cause of all humanity, adding that the adverse effects of global climate change are becoming increasingly apparent.
In light of the new circumstances, Han put forward a four-point proposal.
The first is to stay focused on common goals and strengthen collective action.

He called for the full and effective implementation of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement in accordance with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, so as to rally collective efforts in global climate governance.

Developed countries should take the lead in reducing emissions and fulfill their climate finance commitments, Han said, stressing that all parties should make every effort to implement their nationally determined contributions and strive to do better.
The second is to accelerate the green transition and promote low-carbon development.
Efforts should be made to facilitate the free flow of high-quality green technologies and products, and promote the transformation and upgrading of the economic and industrial structures, Han said.

Noting that China has set targets for 2030, including raising the share of non-fossil energy in total electricity generation to 50 percent and increasing the share of electricity in final energy consumption to 35 percent, Han said that China remains firmly committed to achieving its carbon peak and carbon neutrality goals.
The third is to prevent climate-related disasters and enhance climate resilience.

Equal importance should be attached to mitigation and adaptation, he said, adding that cooperation should be strengthened in areas such as disaster prevention and mitigation, monitoring and early warning, and disaster relief, so as to enhance climate adaptation capacity.
He noted that China is willing to promote the application of its intelligent meteorological early warning solution "MAZU" in more countries, helping them prevent and respond to climate risks.
The fourth is to adhere to openness and inclusiveness and deepen international cooperation.
He said that support and assistance to developing countries should be strengthened to jointly build a clean and beautiful world.

China has continued to promote South-South cooperation projects on climate change, such as the "Africa Solar Belt," and will launch the capacity-building project "Global South climate action leadership program," said the Chinese vice president, noting that China will also contribute to the fair and effective implementation of the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation.

items.title: PLA Air Force marks 77th anniversary amid modernization drive
text: The Red Falcon aerobatics team from the Aviation University of Air Force performs during celebrations to mark the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Nov. 9, 2026. (Xinhua/Yan Linyun)

BEIJING, Nov. 11 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force marked its 77th founding anniversary on Wednesday, highlighting its journey from a modest beginning to a modernizing force with a structure geared toward future operational needs.

In an anniversary video, the Air Force, founded on Nov. 11, 1949, showcased training exercises involving fighter jets, bombers, early warning aircraft, transport planes, helicopters and drones, as well as ground-based air defense missile units, radar units and airborne troops.

The video, released Wednesday on the service's official social media accounts, also highlighted the Air Force's participation in disaster relief and international exchanges, drawing a wave of congratulatory messages.
Anniversary celebrations had begun earlier this month, with events held in different parts of the country.

On Monday morning, eight flight instructors from the Aviation University of the Air Force in Changchun, capital of northeast China's Jilin Province, took to the skies in jet trainers for an aerial display.

That evening, 3,000 drones lit up the sky in a light show depicting the Air Force's evolution, from horse-towed propeller-driven trainer aircraft, to advanced aircraft such as J-20 stealth fighter and Y-20 transport plane.

On Nov. 6, six J-10 jets from the PLA Air Force's Bayi (August 1) Aerobatic Team flew over the Great Wall in north China's Tianjin Municipality as part of the celebrations. The team derives its name from the founding anniversary of the PLA.

"The Great Wall was once a barrier against invaders," said Zha Xiufeng, one of the pilots. "Today, we pilots serve as an 'airborne Great Wall,' safeguarding the peace and security of countless families."
The PLA Air Force started with a small fleet of outdated aircraft. During the founding ceremony of the People's Republic of China on Oct. 1, 1949, only 17 aircraft were available for parade.

In the following years, the Air Force shot down or damaged more than 3,800 enemy aircraft, according to official figures. More than 1,800 Air Force personnel have given their lives in combat operations, scientific research tasks, and dedication to the interests of the people.

The PLA Air Force's three-step development roadmap, issued in 2018, set targets to build a strategic air force by 2020, basically establish a modernized strategic air force by 2035, and become a world-class air force by the middle of the century.
The 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, scheduled to run from Dec. 7 to 13 in Zhuhai, will offer the world a glimpse of the PLA Air Force's latest developments.

items.title: American's decades-long bond with Chinese hometown leaves legacy of kindness
text: XINING, Nov. 11 (Xinhua) -- In 1987, when David V. Plymire first returned to Huangyuan, the plateau county in China he had left decades earlier for the United States, locals were surprised that he still spoke the local dialect fluently.
"I simply talked to myself in front of a mirror so that I wouldn't forget the dialect of my hometown," he later explained to a local journalist.

Born in 1931 in the United States, Plymire spent his formative years with his family in Huangyuan County, now in northwest China's Qinghai Province, before leaving at age 18. Now, the 95-year-old regards the county as his only hometown.
Though an ocean away, Plymire never stopped thinking about the people of Huangyuan. Between 1987 and 2016, he returned more than 20 times, helping improve local health care and education.
To support the once-underdeveloped county, he donated over 30 pieces of medical equipment worth some 6 million yuan (about 895,500 U.S. dollars) to the Huangyuan County People's Hospital.

The donation included a CT scanner worth 350,000 U.S. dollars -- a piece of equipment that no other county-level hospital in Qinghai possessed at the time. The procurement and customs clearance process for the large machine was cumbersome, and only after numerous setbacks did it finally arrive in Huangyuan in 2000.
Standing before the device, Plymire bowed deeply. "This scanner must serve the people of my hometown well," he said in the local dialect.

In 2002, Jia Chengwu, a neurosurgeon from Shenyang, capital of northeast China's Liaoning Province, was dispatched to Huangyuan as part of the country's efforts to promote large-scale development of the western region. There, he performed the county's first craniotomy on a migrant worker with a head injury.

"Without the CT scanner donated by Mr. Plymire, which enabled a timely diagnosis of the worker's intracranial hematoma, I could not have completed that surgery," Jia recalled. "With this batch of donated hardware and the paired assistance from supporting doctors, the hospital became a well-known medical institution in the surrounding area."
Huang Jiong, head of the hospital, said the CT scanner remained in service for 15 years until around 2015, benefiting more than 20,000 people.

The equipment allowed doctors to quickly diagnose hundreds of critically ill patients suffering from cerebral hemorrhage, cerebral infarction and meningitis, securing precious time for surgical rescue and saving numerous lives, Huang said.
In addition to donating medical equipment, Plymire also coordinated with foreign friends to teach English at local schools.
His sister, Mary Ann Plymire, who was born and grew up in Huangyuan, funded the purchase of the county's first ambulance.
In 1998, the Huangyuan county government awarded both of them honorary citizenship.
At Mary's request, her ashes were brought back to the county after she died in 2016, allowing her to rest in peace in the place where she spent her childhood.
The roots of their devotion trace back to their father, Victor G. Plymire, a missionary who arrived in China in 1908 and settled in Huangyuan in 1921.

Modernizing through the Party's self-reform
text: The resolution adopted on Oct 29 at the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China represents far more than an institutional commitment to strengthen Party discipline.

The resolution, which focuses on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance, addresses a fundamental question of contemporary political economy: how can a political organization preserve its capacity to lead profound economic, technological and social transformations while continuously renewing itself?

At a time of rising geopolitical tensions, technological competition and structural changes in the world economy, China's approach places political leadership, institutional capacity and the well-being of the people at the center of its modernization strategy.

One of the most distinctive features of China's development model is the recognition that economic transformation requires a political organization capable of defining long-term objectives, coordinating resources and ensuring their implementation. Markets, technological innovation and industrial competition operate within a broader strategic framework oriented toward national development and collective prosperity.

The resolution thus acquires particular historical significance: it connects the modernization of China's governance system with the political and institutional conditions necessary to advance a new stage of socialist modernization.
The concept of self-reform expresses the CPC's determination to continuously improve its governing capabilities.

Rather than treating institutional strength as an irreversible achievement, self-reform recognizes that political organizations must constantly renew themselves to respond to changing historical circumstances.
The measures stipulated in the resolution seek to prevent corruption, bureaucratism, formalism and the misuse of public authority.
The significance of self-reform therefore extends beyond internal Party organization. It concerns the quality of governance and the capacity to preserve the public purpose of political power.

China has entered a new stage characterized by high-quality development, technological modernization and the pursuit of national rejuvenation. The resolution reflects the CPC's efforts to adapt to evolving international and domestic conditions while maintaining long-term national objectives.
One of the resolution's most important contributions is its emphasis on the comprehensive education, selection, supervision and continuous improvement of Party cadres.

Behind industrial parks, high-speed railways, scientific laboratories and technological breakthroughs lies an extensive organizational structure responsible for translating strategic decisions into concrete results. The resolution calls for cadres who combine political commitment, professional competence, ethical integrity, practical experience and administrative effectiveness. It also emphasizes merit-based selection, accountability, continuous learning and the ability to confront complex problems.

items.title: PLA Air Force marks 77th anniversary amid modernization drive
text: BEIJING -- The Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force marked its 77th founding anniversary on Wednesday, highlighting its journey from a modest beginning to a modernizing force with a structure geared toward future operational needs.

In an anniversary video, the Air Force, founded on Nov 11, 1949, showcased training exercises involving fighter jets, bombers, early warning aircraft, transport planes, helicopters and drones, as well as ground-based air defense missile units, radar units and airborne troops.

The video, released Wednesday on the service's official social media accounts, also highlighted the Air Force's participation in disaster relief and international exchanges, drawing a wave of congratulatory messages.
Anniversary celebrations had begun earlier this month, with events held in different parts of the country.

On Monday morning, eight flight instructors from the Aviation University of the Air Force in Changchun, capital of Northeast China's Jilin province, took to the skies in jet trainers for an aerial display.

That evening, 3,000 drones lit up the sky in a light show depicting the Air Force's evolution, from horse-towed propeller-driven trainer aircraft, to advanced aircraft such as J-20 stealth fighter and Y-20 transport plane.

On Nov 6, six J-10 jets from the PLA Air Force's Bayi (August 1) Aerobatic Team flew over the Great Wall in North China's Tianjin municipality as part of the celebrations. The team derives its name from the founding anniversary of the PLA.

"The Great Wall was once a barrier against invaders," said Zha Xiufeng, one of the pilots. "Today, we pilots serve as an 'airborne Great Wall,' safeguarding the peace and security of countless families."
The PLA Air Force started with a small fleet of outdated aircraft. During the founding ceremony of the People's Republic of China on Oct 1, 1949, only 17 aircraft were available for parade.

In the following years, the Air Force shot down or damaged more than 3,800 enemy aircraft, according to official figures. More than 1,800 Air Force personnel have given their lives in combat operations, scientific research tasks, and dedication to the interests of the people.

The PLA Air Force's three-step development roadmap, issued in 2018, set targets to build a strategic air force by 2020, basically establish a modernized strategic air force by 2035, and become a world-class air force by the middle of the century.
The 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, scheduled to run from Dec 7 to 13 in Zhuhai, will offer the world a glimpse of the PLA Air Force's latest developments.

The Air Force said multiple types of its main combat equipment would make their debut at the show. Equipment for aerial reconnaissance, early warning, air defense, support, airborne operations, unmanned applications and intelligent systems, as well as munitions, will also be displayed at the exhibition.

"Bringing more domestically developed new-generation aircraft closer to the public and taking Air Force stories into households across the country are commitments we will continue to uphold," said Gao Xiang, a senior Air Force official.

items.title: Sun Yat-sen's enduring legacy bridges the Strait
text: Thursday marks the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen, the pioneer of China's democratic revolution and a patriot who dedicated his life to national independence, social progress and the wellbeing of the people.

As a scholar from Taiwan now teaching at a university in Shanghai, I have come to realize that Sun's legacy is not confined to monuments or textbooks. His influence is a quiet, unbroken thread that runs through daily life on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, including my own. For me, Sun is not merely a historical figure, but a living presence connecting the Taiwan of my childhood with the Shanghai of today.

When I was growing up in Taiwan, Sun's presence was everywhere. His portrait was hung above the blackboard in every classroom, watching over us as we began each school day. Nearly every city and town had a Zhongshan Road, a Zhongshan Park or a memorial hall in his honor, and many schools also bore his name, from Zhongshan Elementary School to Zhongshan Junior High School.

Sun's birthday on Nov 12 was a public holiday throughout my childhood. Schools held commemorative assemblies where we paid tribute to his portrait and listened to speeches about his Three Principles of the People: nationalism, civil rights and people's livelihoods.

Sun's thought was woven into our education. In high school, the Three Principles of the People was a compulsory subject tested in the college entrance examination, engaging students from all disciplines with his political philosophy. At university, courses on his thought were mandatory, making it an essential part of understanding China's modern history.

A few years ago, I visited Cuiheng village in Zhongshan city, Guangdong province, where Sun's journey began. Standing before the modest red-brick house he designed and built in 1892 with money sent by his elder brother, I was humbled by the thought of how such a small house could give rise to such a vast historical movement.

In the courtyard grows a tamarind tree he planted as a young man. Though struck by a typhoon decades ago, it refused to die, sprouting new branches from old roots — much like the man himself. In that moment, the great revolutionary became simply a devoted son of the village who loved his country beyond measure.

In Shanghai, I see how his legacy is honored across the Chinese mainland. In Nanjing, capital of Jiangsu province, visitors still climb the 392 stone steps of his mausoleum on Purple Mountain, one for each million of his compatriots at the time, to pay their respects before his resting place.

His name lives on in the streets we walk. In Taipei, I often strolled along Zhongshan North Road, where the Grand Hotel crowns a wooded hill above the Keelung River. In Shanghai, I now walk along Zhongshan East First Road on the Bund, where the colonial-era buildings overlook the Huangpu River. One name, two cities, at opposite sides of the Taiwan Strait. These roads are more than urban landmarks; they are shared spaces of memory, linking two cities that are central to modern Chinese history.

Sun's legacy serves as an important bridge connecting people across the Strait.

During his life, he visited Taiwan three times, in 1900, 1913 and 1918, when the island was under Japanese colonial occupation. items.title: Policy rate shift delivers clarity for mkt
text:
By ZHOU LANXU | 
          China Daily |
          Updated: 2026-11-12 09:03

China's shift to an overnight policy interest rate marks a major step toward completing its price-based monetary policy framework, analysts said, helping clarify policy signals and improve their transmission across financial markets.
Since Nov 2, the People's Bank of China, the country's central bank, has made overnight reverse repurchase operations a daily fixture, replacing seven-day reverse repos as its main routine operation.

Previously conducted during select periods to meet short-term funding needs, overnight operations now take place each working day at a rate of 1.25 percent, with institutions bidding for the amounts they require.

Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, said the operations mean the overnight reverse repo rate has replaced the seven-day reverse repo rate as the PBOC's main policy rate, while seven-day operations now serve as a liquidity management tool deployed as needed.

"With that, China's price-based monetary policy framework is largely complete," Wen said, with DR001 — the overnight pledged repo rate among depository institutions — further confirmed as the central bank's target rate in the money market.

PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng said in October that DR001 had effectively become the central bank's target rate, yet its main open market operations had a seven-day maturity — a mismatch that a shift to overnight operations would address to improve the precision of interest rate management.

According to Wen, the seven-day policy rate incorporated a term premium, meaning it reflected both the central bank's intended interest rate level and its assessment of the premium associated with seven-day funding.
Using an overnight policy rate removes that ambiguity, helping the PBOC keep DR001 close to the policy rate and transmitting clearer signals to other market interest rates, Wen said.

Lou Feipeng, a researcher at Postal Savings Bank of China, said the new framework had been implemented smoothly, with DR001 averaging about 1.28 percent from Nov 2 to Monday — roughly 3 basis points above the new policy rate.
However, DR001 has edged higher this week, reaching 1.327 percent on Wednesday, according to market tracker Wind Info.

Lou attributed the rise to changing funding conditions, including funds drawn out of the interbank market for the Singles' Day shopping festival, midmonth tax payments and government bond settlements, alongside the central bank's net liquidity withdrawals.

Zhang Xu, a fixed-income analyst at Everbright Securities, said in a note that the central bank could guide DR001 slightly higher when bond yields fall too quickly, curbing demand for borrowing to buy bonds and slowing the decline in yields. Zhang interpreted the current rise in DR001 as a signal of the central bank's policy stance.

While analysts highlighted that the policy rate switch should not be interpreted as a rate cut, they acknowledged the scope for the PBOC to take future accommodative steps if needed, even as the US Federal Reserve may continue rate hikes in December following October's higher-than-expected inflation reading.

items.title: Frontier village finds fortune through fortitude after devastating floods
text: Thirty years after floods destroyed their homes, residents of a remote village on China's border with Myanmar are welcoming tourists to the frontier they chose not to leave, selling tropical fruit, opening cafes and finding new ways to earn a living.

The changes in Longli, a Dai village in Daluo township of Yunnan province's Xishuangbanna Dai autonomous prefecture, are echoed in nearby Jinglai, where traditional wooden houses and local crafts have become the foundation of a growing tourism business.

In 1996, floods along the Daluo River destroyed Longli's homes. Rather than relocate closer to the better-equipped township, its 59 households chose to rebuild near the border. They also donated the 60,000 yuan ($8,970) in relocation subsidies to establish a village school.

But determination alone could not overcome isolation. For years, villagers had to travel an extra 6 kilometers to reach town, and fruit buyers were reluctant to collect produce from the village. Farmers often had to accept lower prices.

After returning home in 2019, village Party secretary Yu Ernan began collecting residents' concerns. A 112-meter bridge opened at the end of 2020, shortening journeys and making it easier for agricultural products to reach buyers. Residents then helped improve roads, drainage and public spaces.

Local officials also encouraged farmers to diversify beyond rubber. Party members tried growing dragon fruit before other households followed, and a cooperative helped coordinate cultivation and sales. By 2025, the village had 40 hectares of dragon fruit, with annual output valued at 9 million yuan. Per capita annual income had risen from less than 8,000 yuan to 28,000 yuan, according to local government figures.

In 2023, Longli began working with a tourism company to offer village visits and border-themed experiences. In 2025, it welcomed 127,500 tourist visits and generated about 1.85 million yuan in tourism revenue. More than 30 young people have returned, opening businesses including restaurants and coffee shops.

A monthly market now gives residents, especially older villagers, free stalls to sell homegrown fruit and handicrafts. The market attracted more than 8,000 visits in one month, and participating vendors earn about 1,800 yuan extra per month on average.

Longli's development has also drawn on close community ties. Han, Dai and Blang residents celebrate festivals together, help settle neighborhood disputes and join border patrols. Across the border, about half the village's residents have relatives in Myanmar's Manhui village, with which they maintain cultural exchanges.

In Jinglai, tourism has taken a different route. Once a poor border settlement with per capita annual income below 1,000 yuan, the village began cooperating with a tourism operator in 2003, formalizing a partnership between the village Party branch, the company and residents in 2015.

items.title: Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
text: A pair of Chinese noodle shops serving free meals sparked debate this week after their popularity reportedly disrupted neighboring shops’ business.

“Zero-Yuan Noodle Shop,” which opened two outlets last month in the densely populated Jiangning and Yuhuatai districts of Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, offers only one dish: noodles with braised vegetarian chicken and shiitake mushrooms. Each restaurant has around 50 seats, and since opening have been frequented mainly by middle-aged and elderly customers, according to domestic media.

Jiangning is home to a large migrant worker population, while Yuhuatai has the city’s largest public housing project. Signs outside the restaurants read, “A bowl of pure intention, with no fixed price; three meals a day, offered with warmth to those in need.”

The owner, surnamed Zhang, told domestic media he opened the shops for two reasons: promoting vegetarianism and charity. He said he had previously donated to charities and operated low-cost vegetarian restaurants but found that offering free noodles was the most effective way to achieve his philanthropic goals.

The two shops have served more than 1,000 bowls of noodles each day, Zhang said. He added that he had initially planned to open 10 stores, each serving 500 bowls a day, but demand had exceeded his expectations.
“Our idea was simple: get more people to come eat,” he said.
The topic has garnered more than 10 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many questioning whether the measures can genuinely help those in need.

Asked what they thought about the initiative, a local resident told domestic media, “It’s both good and bad. The good thing is that people who are genuinely struggling can come here to get a meal and meet their basic needs. The bad thing is, how can you tell who has money and who doesn’t?”
Other users suggested requiring customers to show their ID cards to exclude locals and help migrant workers.
In an interview with domestic media, Zhang rejected the idea of screening customers. “We want to give people facing difficulties a sense of dignity and respect,” he said.

Domestic media reported that one nearby restaurant’s daily revenue had fallen from 3,000 yuan ($450) to just a few hundred yuan. Another shop owner said he was considering not renewing his lease over concerns about declining customer traffic.

However, some shop owners said customer traffic along the street had already fallen after the relocation of several nearby factories. Others said the free noodle shops had not significantly affected their business.
Zhang told domestic media that affected business owners could work at his stores if they were willing.
He added that the two shops could lose up to 10 million yuan a year. The stores do not have payment QR codes, and he has also turned down donation offers from friends.

The shops have reportedly recently installed barriers to keep lines orderly and stopped providing noodle refills and napkins to discourage those who don’t truly need help from taking advantage of the offer.

items.title: What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019244/What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
text: Fufeng County, some 110 kilometers west of the northwestern Chinese city of Xi’an, is best known for its stunning Tang dynasty (618–907) relics, unearthed from an underground crypt beneath Famen Temple in the late 1980s.

But ask a Chinese archaeologist about Fufeng, and they’ll likely point you in another direction: toward a quiet cluster of more than 20 villages located along the border with neighboring Qishan County. There, hidden beneath unassuming farms and village houses, lies what a growing number of experts believe was the first capital of the Western Zhou (1046–771 BC) — one of China’s earliest and most important dynasties.

Known as Zhouyuan — literally “The Plains of Zhou” — its excavation sites have produced some of China’s most famous bronze ritual vessels. In the 1940s, those discoveries led archaeologist Shi Zhangru to survey the area and eventually propose that this was Qiyi, the center of Zhou culture before the Zhou toppled the Shang dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BC).

In the decades that followed, archaeologists worked on the site sporadically, uncovering large rammed-earth building foundations, cemeteries, craft workshops, bronze hoards, and oracle bones, all dating to the Zhou period.

Yet planned, continuous excavation at Zhouyuan began only at the turn of the 21st century, when the Institute of Archaeology at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, and Peking University’s School of Archaeology and Museology formed a joint team to systematically explore the site.

Why the delay? Part of the problem was historiographical. Chinese scholars have long relied on written texts to locate historic sites, and for more than 2,000 years historians placed the Western Zhou capital dozens of kilometers away, in a place called Fenghao, near Xi’an.

This drew attention and resources from other sites in the region, including Zhouyuan. But over the past decade or so, the joint archaeological team at Zhouyuan has made a string of breakthroughs that suggest Shi Zhangru’s near-century-old hunch might be right — and possibly even show that Zhouyuan, not Fenghao, was the Western Zhou’s first capital.

“Modern excavations are revealing more and more contradictions between the archaeological record and traditional accounts,” Cao Dazhi, a Peking University-based archaeologist and co-leader of the Zhouyuan team, wrote in a 2023 paper. Cao’s analysis attracted widespread attention in China for arguing that Zhouyuan was the Zhou capital, while the Fenghao region was merely an important hub and site of the royal hunting grounds.
But the dispute over ancient capitals may not be the biggest revelation to emerge from the Zhouyuan excavations.

While the exact significance of the discoveries remains a matter of debate even within the team, mounting evidence suggests the Zhou capital’s population was far more diverse than previously thought. In addition to the core Zhou population, it was home to large numbers of conquered Shang, as well as migrants from the northwest and south.

items.title: ‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019249/‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
text: “Sisters, stand up!” reads a slogan written in pink on the mirror above three pink-and-white urinals. Alongside each sits a stack of disposable paper funnels, waiting for those willing to heed the call.

The scene, reportedly captured in the women’s restroom of a bar in China’s eastern city of Wuxi, began circulating online last week, sparking debate and prompting a related hashtag to garner over 54 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

“I stood there in disbelief for two minutes, thinking I’d walked into the wrong restroom,” one user wrote on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, attaching photos of the urinals. “I kept checking until a cleaner confirmed it was indeed the women’s restroom.”

The user, a Wuxi resident in her 30s surnamed Shi, told domestic media she was unsure how to use the urinals as there were no instructions nearby. She said she eventually opted for a traditional squat toilet in the same restroom instead because she worried about making a mess or soiling her clothes.
“I’d actually love to try this,” one commenter wrote. “In winter, it’s a hassle to squat with all those thick, long layers on, especially when you’re also carrying a bag.”
“Better yet, let the brothers sit down,” read another comment, which received nearly 1,400 likes.

On Tuesday, a woman surnamed Tang, who runs Gungun Folk Theater, the bar where the urinals were reportedly installed, told domestic media that they were intended for women who find it difficult to squat, including those wearing long dresses or with limited mobility. “We just wanted to make things easier and give women another option,” she said.

Studies suggest that standing to urinate may be easier for pregnant women and those with knee osteoarthritis, while standing, crouching, and sitting have been found to make no significant difference to bladder emptying in healthy women.
Standing urinals are increasingly common worldwide at music festivals to save space and reduce restroom queues, and at outdoor activities where toilets are scarce.

In China, efforts to introduce standing urinals for women reportedly date back to 2004. At that time, Ye Ganlin, a retired senior engineer, spent 10,000 yuan ($1,400) developing a portable standing urinal for all genders, and offered free disposable funnels to female users. She said the idea grew out of her own experience with a spinal condition that made squatting increasingly difficult as she aged.

Her toilet was tested in busy public areas of neighboring cities Xi’an and Xianyang, in the northwestern Shaanxi province, and reportedly drew around 200 users a day. However, women were in the minority, Ye said.

In 2010, Shaanxi Normal University, also in Xi’an, installed six standing urinals for women, an initiative championed by professor Qu Yajun to conserve water. Female students welcomed the idea but said it would take practice to get used to the fixtures.

text: The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) closed in Shanghai on Tuesday after showcasing cutting-edge technologies in artificial intelligence, commercial aerospace, and innovative drugs.

The six-day event drew exhibitors from a record 162 countries, regions, and international organizations. A total of 4,142 overseas companies took part — also a record high — with more than 480 representative products making their global, Asian, or China debut.

The prototype will provide the foundation for 6G chips and support the technology’s commercial rollout.

The event featured an expanded medical devices and health care exhibition area, acting as the stage for the China debut of pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca’s new hypertension medication baxdrostat. The oral medication works by inhibiting the enzyme aldosterone synthase, which helps synthesize the blood pressure-regulating hormone aldosterone, and was approved in the U.S. in May.

German optical giant Zeiss also made its global debut of its new non-spherical lens PT Lunana, designed for myopia correction. Novartis, a Swiss multinational pharmaceutical company, showcased ianalumab, a drug used for treating the autoimmune illness Sjögren’s disease — also a China debut.

American electric vehicle company Tesla presented its Cybercab autonomous vehicle. Lacking a steering wheel or pedals, the vehicle relies on cameras and AI to drive. Hexagon — a global digital reality and metrology tech company — also displayed its industrial humanoid robot AEON.

Aerospace technology was also present, including the Zhuque-3 rocket developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company LandSpace. The rocket’s reusable booster, which uses liquid oxygen and methane as fuel, can land vertically, first achieved by the company in August.

Beyond showcasing new tech, the expo held its first exhibition area for 100 long-established, reputable international brands — from Canadian shoe companies to Spanish wineries — as well as hosted a trade and investment “matchmaking” conference, where companies and buyers met to sign cooperation agreements. The latter conference attracted more than 600 exhibitors and over 2,000 buyers from 59 countries and regions.
The deals reached at this year’s expo are projected to be worth a total of $85.45 billion over the coming year, up 2.3% from last year and a record high.

items.title: Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019239/Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
text: China has opened its first school dedicated to declining and obscure fields of study, with a focus on ancient and classical Chinese texts.

The School for Rare and Endangered Disciplines was inaugurated in Beijing on Nov. 6 under the University of Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (UCASS). At the opening, the university also announced the launch of a national alliance of more than 80 universities, museums, and cultural and research institutions to share resources, conduct collaborative research, and cultivate talent in related fields.

The school comes as the number of scholars studying ancient Chinese scripts dwindles. Nationwide, only about 500 people work in ancient Chinese writing studies, and of the roughly 4,500 known oracle bone characters — the oldest known fully developed form of Chinese writing and widely used for divination purposes during the Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) — nearly two-thirds remain undeciphered, underlining the need for further research.

The initiative also builds on previous attempts by UCASS to preserve such fields, such as establishing an institute for rare and endangered studies in 2024 to train future talent in fields such as bamboo and silk studies, which examines script on the two materials, as well as classical studies, Turkic studies, and Assyriology, or studies of the Ancient Near East.

Each student of the new school’s bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degree courses will be mentored by two members of the school’s more than 140 faculty members. UCASS has also built dedicated laboratories for the school’s use.

Students may pursue research in oracle bone studies, bamboo and silk studies, and classical studies. They may also train in over 10 ancient ethnic scripts, including Turkic, Tangut, Khitan, Jurchen, Manchu, Old Tibetan, Old Yi, Phags-pa, Naxi Dongba, and Zhuang.

“Ancient scripts like oracle bone script are on the verge of being lost, and some frontier history research relies on the survival of the country’s cultural roots and its long-term development,” Huang Dekuan, director of the Research and Conservation Center for Unearthed Texts at Tsinghua University, told state broadcaster CCTV.
Such disciplines are also hampered by scattered resources and research institutions working in isolation — key obstacles to research and transmission, according to CCTV.

China has called for increased focus on cultural heritage preservation in recent years. At an October press conference on cultural heritage protection, government officials called for advancing cultural heritage as a discipline, cultivating interdisciplinary talent in the field, and encouraging qualified universities to establish cultural heritage schools.

In a Nov. 7 commentary, domestic media outlet The Beijing News wrote that by emphasizing rare and endangered disciplines, the new school offers a lesson to other universities: schools should develop their own distinctive majors, resist the urge to offer only popular fields, and actively strengthen less mainstream majors.
“Only then can a university truly serve education,” it stated.

items.title: Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019245/Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
text: Coming from a Shanghai family with a strong academic background, Yang Fan had always felt studying at university was his destiny. The only problem was, he was flunking middle school.

“He’d make the same mistake with a character the entire semester. I just couldn’t get him to do it right,” says his mother, Zhao Xuan, who could only look on in frustration as Yang struggled with his homework night after night. “Given how much it was taking for him to get through middle school, I felt high school would crush him.”

Last summer, with the conventional academic pathway looking a bad fit for their 15-year-old son, Zhao and her husband began to consider China’s integrated secondary vocational-to-undergraduate articulation program. Launched as a 2014 pilot in Shanghai, the initiative sees students spend up to three years at a vocational school before transitioning to a partner university to complete a related four-year bachelor’s degree program.
Over the past 12 years, the number of participating educational institutions has rapidly expanded, now covering at least seven provincial regions, and applications have soared.

Shanghai alone has established 91 majors across 38 vocational schools and 18 universities, enrolling about 20,000 students and producing six cohorts of graduates. Planned enrollment this year was 2,756, up from just 120 in 2014 and a 17.5% increase from 2025.

Programs cover diverse fields including robotics, accounting, digital media arts, big data engineering, logistics, environmental design, hospitality management, cultural heritage restoration, smart manufacturing, performing arts, sound recording, information security, and materials science.

The trend reflects a sea change in attitudes toward vocational education in China. Technical skills training has long been stigmatized as “low status” and a “fallback option,” but as the country’s workforce undergoes a massive restructuring driven by an aging population, advancements in artificial intelligence, and an economic slowdown, more people feel it now makes students more employable compared to those with purely academic backgrounds.

In real terms, most students in the integrated program say their experiences are far less stressful than those of their peers at traditional Chinese high schools, and that they are encouraged to focus more on their personal strengths rather than sticking to a one-size-fits-all curriculum.

However, because most applicants are only in their mid-teens, it’s often parents who make the final decision, with research suggesting that more-passive children have only a vague idea of, or interest in, what might lie ahead.

It was only when Zhao learned that the prestigious Shanghai Maritime University (SMU) would join the integrated secondary vocational-to-undergraduate articulation program in 2026 that she was sure the pathway was a “realistic match” for Yang.

items.title: More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019236/More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
text: More Chinese regions are implementing autumn and spring breaks in compulsory education, expanding a decadelong national initiative. Some have also waived fees for students on break and rolled out support measures to help parents take leave at the same time as their children.

Spring and autumn holidays across all compulsory education schools have been rolled out provincewide in at least 15 provinces, as well as numerous cities in other provinces, such as the southern megacity of Shenzhen, domestic media reported last week. In China, compulsory education lasts nine years, encompassing primary and middle school. Breaks will occur in November and April for four to five days each.

The reform dates back to 2004, when Hangzhou, capital of the eastern province of Zhejiang, piloted the breaks. In 2013, the initiative expanded nationally when the State Council issued an announcement encouraging local governments to adopt it, and the rollout accelerated again in 2025 when central authorities urged more schools to implement the holidays.
Chu Zhaohui, a researcher at the China National Academy of Educational Sciences, told domestic media outlet Red Star News that the holidays actually boost learning.
“Learning isn’t confined to schools or taught only by teachers and parents,” Chu said, adding that the holidays give students space for self-exploration.

At the same time as introducing spring and autumn holiday policies, many cities have also added supporting measures so parents can sync their leave. In October, Longnan city in the northwestern Gansu province encouraged employers to implement paid leave and prioritize compensatory rest for employees with school-age children, aligning staff leave with school holidays.

Foshan, a city in the southern Guangdong province, also issued a proposal on Nov. 3 calling on employers to prioritize arranging leave for employees with children during the autumn holiday. The city’s five-day autumn break begins Nov. 11.

Many tourist spots are also waiving entrance fees for children during the upcoming fall break. In the eastern city of Wuxi, a theme park dropped entry fees for students 16 and under throughout November; 15 top tourism sites in Huangshan in the eastern Anhui province, a city known for its mountain of the same name, are now entry-free for children under 18; and the Dujiangyan scenic area in the southwestern Sichuan province waived fees for primary and middle school students between Nov. 12 and 16.

The breaks have significantly boosted travel demand, according to online travel booking platform Qunar. Data from Qunar revealed that in November, air ticket bookings for children 12 and under increased 1.6 times year on year, while parent bookings rose by 50%.

Wang Qiyan, director of the Leisure Economy Research Center at Renmin University, told Red Star News that spring and autumn breaks “enable off-peak travel, avoiding the packed scenic spots of winter and summer vacations.

items.title: China's NEV exports surge 144.7% in Oct, growth expected to moderate as overseas markets mature
text: China's new-energy vehicle (NEV) exports surged 144.7 percent year-on-year in October, industry data showed on Monday, underscoring strong overseas demand even as domestic sales weakened. Industry analysts said that exports are likely to maintain robust momentum in the near term, although growth is likely to moderate as overseas markets mature and competition intensifies.

Chinese producers exported 582,000 passenger NEVs in October, up 3.9 percent from September, according to data released by the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). Meanwhile, domestic NEV retail sales fell 13.7 percent year-on-year to 1.109 million units, although they rose 2.3 percent month-on-month.
Cui Dongshu, secretary-general of the CPCA, told the Global Times on Monday that China's automobile exports are expected to shift from rapid growth this year to a more moderate pace in 2027.

Cui forecast that overall vehicle export growth could slow to about 10 percent next year as shipments to Russia stabilize and exports to the EU face mounting pressure. The Middle East region could provide additional growth, although prospects remain uncertain, he said.
Passenger NEV exports reached 4.472 million units in the first 10 months of 2026, up 139.7 percent year-on-year, according to the CPCA.

These figures also point to a changing export structure. NEVs accounted for 62.8 percent of China's passenger vehicle exports in October, up 20 percentage points from a year earlier. Battery electric vehicles represented 61.7 percent of NEV shipments, while conventional plug-in hybrids accounted for 33.7 percent.

Leading Chinese automakers recorded substantial overseas shipments. BYD exported 165,194 passenger NEVs in October, followed by Chery with 83,843 and Geely with 80,119, CPCA figures showed. Tesla China's exports reached 59,012 units.

Zhang Xiang, a researcher at the Automotive Industry Innovation Research Center of North China University of Technology, told the Global Times on Monday that Chinese automakers have established a competitive edge in the global NEV market through technological advances, mature supply chains and increasingly competitive products.

He said that he expects overseas demand to remain strong in the coming months, supporting continued export growth. However, as NEV adoption expands and initial demand is gradually absorbed, export growth is likely to return to a more sustainable pace over the longer term.

The expansion comes amid a changing international trade environment. The EU has imposed additional countervailing duties on China-made battery electric vehicles, while Chinese manufacturers are increasingly exploring emerging markets to diversify their overseas sales.

According to the International Energy Agency, sales of Chinese-made electric cars last year grew by 130 percent in Southeast Asia, 60 percent in the Middle East and 55 percent in Latin America, highlighting growing demand beyond traditional markets.

items.title: Singapore Business Federation leads 54 firms to CIIE to unlock bilateral and regional opportunities
text: Singapore firms continue to value China as an important market, and the Southeast Asian country's extensive business networks and familiarity with Southeast Asian markets make it a valuable partner for Chinese enterprises looking to expand their regional footprint, an executive of the Singapore Business Federation said.

China remains a significant market for Singapore businesses, underpinned by its vast consumer market, evolving demand and focus on high-quality development, Mark Lee, chairman of SBF, said during an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the ongoing 9th China International Import Expo held in Shanghai on Friday.

The federation is leading a delegation of 54 Singapore firms to the CIIE. Since the inaugural CIIE in 2018, Singapore businesses have generated about 2.79 billion yuan ($420 million) in cumulative trade value through the event.

Spanning established household names and emerging businesses, participating Singaporean firms at the expo highlight the country's competitive strength in food, health and wellness, consumer innovation, financial services and professional solutions.

They include See Hai Tat Medical Hall (Singapore) Pte Ltd, which looks to grow its consumer presence in China, and Prima Food Pte Ltd, which wants to use the CIIE to explore opportunities in the Chinese market.

With Singapore set to be the ASEAN chair in 2027, the SBF's participation in the CIIE this year — as it has done across all previous editions of the expo — further highlights its role as a strategic bridge for Chinese enterprises looking to expand into the ASEAN market, Lee said.

"Singapore features transparent, trusted legal frameworks and strong intellectual property protection, which helps safeguard technology rights as solutions expand into ASEAN and other regions. We are also a financing hub," Lee said, adding that this explains why many of the country's professional services partners are at the CIIE. They include banks, advisory firms, human resources consultants, legal service providers and trade compliance specialists.

He highlighted that China is among the global leaders in AI and digitization. Singaporean businesses want to work closely and conduct business with their Chinese counterparts, and such collaborations are already underway.

Lee raised the example of Pony.ai, a Chinese autonomous vehicle AI company, which partnered with ComfortDelGro, a Singaporean transport operator that runs taxi and fleet services. They launched a robotaxi pilot in China's Guangzhou, Guangdong province, and following the pilot, a robotaxi service was rolled out earlier this year in a designated area in Singapore, using Pony.ai's technology.

"ComfortDelGro stated that the pilot supports its broader global strategy covering China and Singapore, since it provides fleet management services across multiple markets. This illustrates a strong model: proven Chinese technology, localized by Singapore companies, with plans to scale into other regions and countries," Lee said.
Singapore and China share longstanding economic ties, with bilateral trade in goods reaching approximately 895.9 billion yuan last year

items.title: Record number of product debuts at CIIE highlights China’s emerging role as innovation hub
text: "Show China your best." That is the invitation the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) extends to the world. The response? More than 480 products and technologies making their global, Asian or China debuts, from 6G device prototypes and AI computing systems to innovative medicines, luxury skincare and fragrances - a vibrant showcase of global innovation meeting the energy of China's vast consumer market that is more open to new products and ideas.

For global companies, the CIIE is more than a showcase for new products. It is a window into China - one that opens onto a vast consumer market, an evolving innovation landscape and expanding opportunities for international cooperation. What comes through that window is not just a flow of goods, but a deeper exchange of ideas, technologies and opportunities.

At Qualcomm's booth in the Technology and Equipment Exhibition Area, visitors are lining up to see what the US chipmaker describes as the world's first 6G device prototype compliant with the latest 3GPP specifications. Making its global debut at the expo, the prototype is among the booth's main attractions.

Another new arrival is the large-model-native agent phone STEPX Neo, which integrates applications and services including Alipay, Jianying (CapCut) and Trip.com. Its combination of hardware, software and AI models points to how AI agents could become more closely integrated into everyday mobile services.

Intel is taking a different approach to the AI boom, focusing on where computing power is generated and how it is supplied. Its CIIE debut is a computing solution that places computing clusters inside shipping containers, with flexible energy storage modules, allowing them to operate closer to renewable energy sources.

"Rather than bringing electricity to computing centers, it makes more sense to move computing clusters closer to where the electricity is generated," Intel China Chairman Wang Zhicong told the Global Times.
The solution, first conceived as an idea at last year's expo, combines computing power, renewable energy and storage, with Chinese energy and IT companies involved in its development.

The exhibits are not confined to technology and equipment. In healthcare, Roche is presenting nearly 100 debut and first-show exhibits, including innovative medicines for breast cancer, lupus nephritis and other diseases. Boehringer Ingelheim is showcasing 14 innovative pipeline products and solutions in human pharmaceuticals and animal health, with three therapies at the forefront of global R&D making their China debut.

Both companies are also looking to deepen their engagement with China's medical innovation ecosystem. Vivian Bian, CEO of Roche Pharma China, told the Global Times that Roche will take the CIIE as an important fulcrum for open cooperation, continue to increase its local investment, and deeply integrate into China's medical innovation ecosystem.

Over the last half a century, Chinese spies have taken aim at a wide swath of California targets.

They have worked as a Boeing aerospace engineer and a naval engineer at defense contractor Power Paragon to obtain highly classified information on U.S. space shuttle and Navy projects. They have assumed the roles of electrical engineering professor at UCLA and software engineer at Google and even worked as a driver and aide to  the late U.S. Sen. Dianne Feinstein when she chaired the Senate Intelligence Committee.

Intelligence experts say that China continues to ramp up its network of spies and assets across California, as underscored this week after Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang admitted he was embroiled in an extramarital affair when allegations surfaced that he had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

“For years, the FBI has been sounding the alarm regarding China’s ambitious efforts to gain technological, economic and geopolitical superiority,” said former Assistant Chief Horace Frank of the Los Angeles Police Department, who oversaw intelligence. “Their activities constitute a long-term strategic threat — not only to the United States, but to the world. Their counterintelligence strategy is not only about stealing secrets today; it’s about securing strategic advantages tomorrow. They recognize that human vulnerabilities (sex, money, ego and ambition) can be crucial when it comes to them attaining this quest for global dominance.”

For China, California is a key espionage hub because it combines three attractive targets: advanced technology industries, major research universities and a large concentration of scientists, engineers and entrepreneurs, according to William Hannas, lead analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. China’s main objectives are to accelerate its technological development, reduce dependence on foreign suppliers and achieve leadership in strategically important fields, including artificial intelligence, Hannas said.
“Silicon Valley is especially important,” he  said, “because it offers access not only to existing technologies, but also to innovations at their earliest stages.”
California is also a focal point of China’s espionage efforts, some experts say, because it has the highest number of Chinese residents in the continental U.S.

items.title: China warns US not to use Nvidia scandal as pretext for tech curbs
China Slams ‘Chinese Spy Narrative’ And Warns Against Push For U.S. Chip Curbs Amid Nvidia Scandal
Lutnick should ban Chinese memory maker CXMT from U.S., Sen. Cotton says
text: Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., is urging the Trump administration to take a harsher stance toward Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies.

"CXMT, one of Communist China's national memory chip champions, poses a growing risk to our economic prosperity and military superiority," Cotton wrote in a letter sent Thursday to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. "The U.S. must take action to prevent CXMT from gaining a stronger foothold in the global market."
CXMT is the world's fourth-largest producer of DRAM  – or dynamic random access memory – which powers many basic functions of computers and smartphones.

Cotton, in a letter first obtained by CNBC, is asking Lutnick to push CXMT onto the department's Bureau of Industry and Security Entity List, which would significantly restrict U.S. firms' ability to do business with the company.

"It basically means that U.S. companies are not allowed to do business with that entity-listed company, and that entity-listed company does not get access to U.S. technology," said Kyle Chan, a Brookings Institution fellow who studies China's technology development.
DRAM is a "commodity," MS Hwang, research director at Counterpoint, told CNBC, meaning it is made to a global standard and is generally interchangeable from one manufacturer to another.

However, with the right production technology, it can also form the building blocks of HBM, or high-bandwidth memory. HBM is an extremely high-demand product that powers AI chips made by Nvidia, Google and Amazon Web Services, which are central to the growth of artificial intelligence giants including Anthropic and OpenAI. It's made by just three main companies: Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron.

Those same three companies control the lion's share of the DRAM market, but CXMT has made inroads. The company's share of the DRAM market jumped from 4% to 10% by revenue in a year, from the second quarter of 2025 to the same quarter of 2026, according to Counterpoint using the most recent reporting available. And in July, the company went public and its stock price soared, making it the most valuable company listed in China at the time.

While the company's HBM capabilities are nascent, according to Counterpoint, Reuters reported that the company was to begin production of the chips, even though yields are low at just 20% to 30%. That means that the majority of the chips it produces are faulty.

CXMT is already on the Pentagon's "1260H" list, which identifies several dozen Chinese companies with ties to Beijing's military. But Chan says that list doesn't come with stringent restrictions for U.S. businesses.
"It's not a list that has that much teeth to it, in terms of restrictions to U.S. companies working with Chinese firms on that list," Chan said.

The Wall Street Journal reported Aug. 9 that Apple was considering using CXMT's memory in iPhones and Macs in light of the global shortage driven by the AI buildout. Being on the Entity List could change that.
