items.title: In China’s Spy Operations, Romance Can Be a Long Game
text: At the height of the Cold War, a top official in China’s intelligence agency said that his country would never use seduction to entrap a person.

Such tactics might be for the C.I.A. or the K.G.B., the official named Kong Yuan, of the Central Investigation Department, told a group of agents in training in April 1960, but China was guided by principles. He looked at the few female comrades in the audience. “Rest assured, we will not be asking you to go run beauty traps.”

Despite that pledge, captured in a 2010 memoir by a former Chinese diplomat, China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people.

American officials say that China’s Ministry of State Security, which runs intelligence operations today, recruited a Chinese businesswoman to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia and one of the most powerful figures in the artificial intelligence boom.

It was not clear what role the woman, Alice Huang, or Huang Le, might have had with the Chinese spy agency. Ms. Huang was a top executive of a Singapore company that operates data centers in Southeast Asia using Nvidia chips and that rents their computing power to Chinese firms.

Mr. Huang has acknowledged that he had an affair with Ms. Huang. President Trump has said that Mr. Huang told him that he was not aware that the woman was a spy. China has rejected the espionage allegations against Ms. Huang, calling them smears against the country. U.S. officials have not provided evidence for their claims. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

The use of relationships or seduction in the world of espionage is not new or unique to China. The tactic was made infamous by East Germany’s “Romeos,” male Stasi agents tasked with seducing the clerks of Western officials, and by the Soviet Union’s longtime use of sexual blackmail, among other examples.

What is unique about China’s use of the tactic is the amount of time invested, according to Nicholas Eftimiades, a retired senior American intelligence officer who writes about China’s espionage operations.
“They play this long term,” he said. “These are long-term relationships, sometimes marriages.”

Perhaps the most famous example involves Shi Peipu, a Peking Opera singer whose two-decade relationship with Bernard Boursicot, who worked on French diplomatic missions in Beijing and Ulan Bator in Mongolia, drew Mr. Boursicot into spying for China. Both were arrested in France, at which point Mr. Boursicot learned that his lover was a man. In 1986, they were convicted of espionage. Their story inspired the play “M. Butterfly” by David Henry Hwang.

More recent cases include Christine Fang, or Fang Fang, who was believed by counterintelligence officials to be a Chinese spy and who was in a physical relationship with former U.S. Representative Eric Swalwell between 2012 and 2015.

items.title: China’s Xi says Taiwan ‘reunification’ must happen as history cannot be stopped
text: BEIJING — The tide of history cannot be stopped, Chinese President Xi Jinping said Thursday, as he urged complete “reunification” of Taiwan with the motherland and pledged to do so peacefully, making no mention of the use of force.

China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, despite Taipei’s strong rejection of that claim, and has repeatedly offered a “one country, two systems” model of autonomy not supported by any major Taiwanese political party.
Resolving the Taiwan question is an “unwavering historical mission” of China’s Communist Party, Xi said in a speech in Beijing’s Great Hall of the People.
“The tide of history cannot be stopped,” Xi added. “The complete reunification of the motherland must be realized, and it will certainly be realized.”
Taiwan’s government dismissed the remarks as nothing new.
“As for the wording on Taiwan unification, it isn’t much different from the past,” said Liang Wen-chieh, spokesperson for Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council.

Xi’s comments came in a speech on the 160th birthday of revolutionary hero Sun Yat-sen, who helped lead a 1911 revolt that ended centuries of rule by emperors and empresses and ushered in the Republic of China.

China Says US Should Not Use Huang Scandal to Justify Tech Curbs
China's Ministry of State Security thrust into the spotlight by Nvidia CEO affair
text: From recruitment of U.S. students to allegations surrounding Nvidia's Jensen Huang affair, reports point to one Chinese intelligence agency: the Ministry of State Security.

The opaque government entity — which lacks an official website other than one supporting whistleblowers — has gained prominence with Beijing's growing emphasis on national security since 2023. The ministry oversees a range of provincial and national-level bureaus, including for intelligence gathering.

While the MSS is not Beijing's only intelligence entity, the ministry has often been named in high-profile cases. Following hacking attempts on U.S. entities, the U.S. Treasury Department has in recent years sanctioned Chinese entities and individuals it alleges are affiliated with MSS.

The Financial Times and The New York Times this month reported, citing sources, that U.S. government intelligence believe the MSS recruited businesswoman Alice Huang to gather information on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The two are not related. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair over the weekend, but it remains unclear whether any sensitive information was shared.

The MSS earlier this year approached an individual who knows Alice Huang — to find out more information about her business and connections, The FT reported Wednesday, citing the person who was questioned. The FT report said it was unclear whether she was suspected of any wrongdoing, and that the MSS inquiry followed news of a Singapore probe into the company related to chip-smuggling allegations.

China established its Ministry of State Security in 1983, in part to respond to risks from the country's new openness to foreigners after roughly three decades of tightly closed borders, according to research by Sheena Chestnut Greitens, an associate professor at the University of Texas-Austin.

The MSS appears to have gained political influence under Chinese President Xi Jinping to "strengthen China's protections against espionage and foreign infiltration," Greitens wrote last year in China Leadership Monitor. The publication is run by Minxin Pei, non-resident senior fellow of the German Marshall Fund of the United States.

In 2023 MSS launched a social media account on the WeChat messaging platform to increase public awareness of security issues. An article published Tuesday criticized an unidentified individual with a Chinese surname for fabricating allegations to a foreign organization that a colleague was a spy, after learning the colleague had secured an overseas posting that the individual had wanted.
China's MSS is separate from China's Cyberspace Administration as well as the Ministry of Public Security, whose Minister Wang Xiaohong met with then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken.

But the entities can work together. In September, State Security Minister Chen Yixin published a rare article in the cyberspace regulator's magazine about the need to improve artificial intelligence governance and prevent related security risks. The piece came out just as prominent U.S. AI company executives warned about the risks from uncontrolled development of the technology.

Jensen Huang's affair with alleged spy revives push to tighten China chip curbs ahead of Trump-Xi summit
text: The scandal engulfing Nvidia Corp CEO Jensen Huang is bolstering the case for U.S. lawmakers seeking tighter restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips, just days before President Donald Trump's planned meeting with Xi Jinping next week.

The U.S. and China are locked in a race to achieve global AI supremacy, with Washington spending years restricting China's access to Nvidia's most advanced chips to slow its technological progress. Huang was among the loudest voices opposing U.S. strict export controls on advanced chips to China, which has irked some China hawks.

The alleged affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen who is not related to him and was reportedly recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information, has given lawmakers fresh ammunition to push for the inclusion of a series of chip-control measures in this year's National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).
The bills include the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act – all of which are aimed at limiting the flow of advanced chips to U.S. adversaries, particularly China.

Huang had been "the industry's most effective lobbyist against tighter rules," said David Meale, head of Eurasia Group's China practice and an American diplomat who served as deputy chief of mission at the U.S. embassy in Beijing.

But the scandal has weakened Nvidia's "singular ability to slow the progress of those bills" — which were stalled by pushback from corporates and the White House— and made it "politically harder for negotiators to strip chip provisions out of this year's NDAA," Meale said.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer on Tuesday called on Congress to pass these bills and urged a full accounting of Trump's defense of Huang. House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., also called for inclusion of chip export controls in the annual defense policy bill.

Trump's weakened grip over congressional Republicans following the midterm defeat has also made it harder for the Trump administration to hold back such measures, said Kyle Chan, a China fellow at the Brookings Institution.
The fallout from Jensen Huang's affair threatens to put fresh scrutiny on offshore data-center hubs that provide Chinese customers with access to Nvidia chips restricted for direct export to China.
Alice Huang helped facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to China, according to The Information.

Short seller firm Culper Research estimated in May that more than 20% of Nvidia's revenue for the year ended July 2025, or about $43.2 billion, came from China through illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries.

Pressure is building in the White House for Trump to address remote access to restricted chips, and action "now appears likely," said Gabriel Wildau, managing director at political risk consultancy Teneo. Potential escalations include blacklisting Megaspeed and other entities, and introducing rules that close the loophole entirely, he said.
